title: Dolphins Eavesdrop on Their Prey—and Each Other
gist: A PeerJ study finds dolphins may eavesdrop on sound-producing fish like drums (Sciaenidae), which quiet down in dolphins' presence, adding a new layer to the acoustic competition dolphins already face from human ocean noise.

insights.claim: A study published in PeerJ found that dolphins may eavesdrop on fish such as drums (family Sciaenidae), which vocalize by vibrating their swim bladders but become quieter when dolphins are present.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Suggests a previously undocumented predator-prey acoustic dynamic in coastal marine ecosystems, of interest to marine bioacoustics research rather than markets.
insights.quote: dolphins may be eavesdropping on fishes that make sound, such as drums (Sciaenidae) that croak by vibrating their swim bladders but are known to become quieter in the presence of dolphin sounds
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Adding to the acoustic melee...'

insights.claim: Human-made ocean noise—from oil drilling, ship traffic, and explosives—increasingly impairs dolphin communication, which relies on whistles for social interaction and rapid-fire echolocation clicks for navigating and finding prey.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Flags a documented environmental pressure point relevant to offshore energy/shipping activity and marine-noise regulation discussions.
insights.quote: dolphins have to compete with a ton of different human-made noises, from oil drilling to ship traffic to explosives, that impair their communication

insights.claim: Florida Atlantic University's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute researchers used a wave glider towing an underwater recorder suspended 4 to 10 meters below the surface to listen to dolphins for two months along the Atlantic Coast from Fort Pierce to Jacksonville.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Describes the methodology (autonomous wave glider recording) used to generate the study's underlying data.
